review.calculation_check: Independently calculated μ₀ε₀ = 1.1121238 × 10⁻¹⁷ s²/m² and c = 2.9986338 × 10⁸ m/s, which rounds to 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s. The displayed intermediate square-root discrepancy is immaterial rounding.
review.assumptions: Vacuum propagation using the stated rounded SI constants; the displayed permeability is sufficiently accurate for this calculation.
review.notes: Correct relation, units, and numerical verification of the vacuum speed of light.
review.reviewer: Codex CLI paced physics reasoning review

items.preview: Show that, when SI units for $${\mu }_{0} $$ and $${\epsilon }_{0} $$ are entered, the units given by the right-hand side of the equation in the problem above are m/s.

review.reasoning_check: The solution correctly expands tesla, newton, and coulomb into base units and cancels the mass and current dimensions. This establishes dimensional consistency, although dimensional consistency alone cannot establish a physical law or its numerical coefficient.
review.calculation_check: [μ₀] = kg·m·A⁻²·s⁻² and [ε₀] = A²·s⁴·kg⁻¹·m⁻³. Their product is s²/m², so its inverse square root has units m/s.
review.assumptions: Standard SI unit definitions. The historical assertion about dimensional consistency giving Maxwell personal confidence was not independently established by the supplied evidence.
review.notes: The requested dimensional derivation is correct; the historical confidence claim remains unverified.
review.reviewer: Codex CLI paced physics reasoning review

items.preview: ::: example {"id":"Example1","class":"example"} Calculating $$B $$ -Field Strength in an Electromagnetic Wave What is the maximum strength of the $$B $$ -field in an electromagnet…

review.reasoning_check: A freely propagating vacuum wave has E₀ = cB₀, so the maximum magnetic field follows directly from the maximum electric field. Geometric spreading reduces both amplitudes. The Earth-field comparison is reasonable using the textbook's representative terrestrial field of approximately 50 μT.
review.calculation_check: B₀ = 1000/(3.00 × 10⁸) = 3.333 × 10⁻⁶ T. Also, (V/m)/(m/s) = V·s/m² = T. Relative to 50 μT, this is 0.0667, less than one tenth.
review.assumptions: A traveling wave in vacuum or approximately in air, rather than a standing wave or antenna near field. The Earth-field comparison uses a representative value and is not universal at every location.
review.notes: Correct field amplitude and spreading discussion within the traveling-wave model.
review.reviewer: Codex CLI paced physics reasoning review

items.preview: The direction of the electric field shown in each part of [[Figure 1]](#Figure1) is that produced by the charge distribution in the wire. Justify the direction shown in each part,…

review.reasoning_check: Inspection of Figure 1 confirms the stated charge signs and arrows. Beside the symmetric antenna midpoint, repulsion from the positive lower end and attraction toward the negative upper end both contribute upward force in (a) and (d). Reversing the charges reverses that force in (c). In the figure's prescribed charge-separation model, the Coulomb contribution vanishes in (b). The outward-moving arrows represent earlier phases rather than the instantaneous local charge distribution.
review.calculation_check: For endpoint charges ±Q a distance a above and below the midpoint, the transverse components cancel and the axial field magnitude is 2kQa/(r² + a²)^(3/2), with the stated directions. At 100 MHz, T = 10⁻⁸ s and cT = 3.00 m.
review.assumptions: The simplified Coulomb-field schematic explicitly used by the problem. Instantaneous neutrality does not generally imply zero total electric field around a real time-dependent antenna, whose induction and radiation fields require retarded electrodynamics.
review.notes: All four panels are explained correctly within the supplied schematic; the neutrality argument applies to its charge-separation contribution.
review.reviewer: Codex CLI paced physics reasoning review

items.preview: Is the direction of the magnetic field shown in [[Figure 2]](#Figure2) (a) consistent with the right-hand rule for current (RHR-2) in the direction shown in the figure?

review.reasoning_check: Figure 2(a) shows upward conventional current and magnetic arrows pointing right on the near side. For upward current, the right-hand rule gives counterclockwise circulation viewed from above. With the stated right-handed coordinates, ŷ × ẑ = x̂ independently confirms the near-side direction.
review.calculation_check: The illustrative long-wire calculation gives B = (4π × 10⁻⁷)(1.00)/(2π × 0.100) = 2.00 × 10⁻⁶ T, as stated.
review.assumptions: The numerical illustration additionally assumes a sufficiently long straight wire and a quasistatic observation region. These assumptions are unnecessary for the basic right-hand-rule direction check.
review.notes: The inspected magnetic arrows agree with the current direction and right-hand rule.
review.reviewer: Codex CLI paced physics reasoning review

items.preview: Why is the direction of the current shown in each part of [[Figure 2]](#Figure2) opposite to the electric field produced by the wire’s charge separation?

review.reasoning_check: The directional explanation matches Figure 2: upward conventional current builds positive charge at the top, while the resulting charge-separation field points downward. However, the added example incorrectly identifies qV with generator work per AC cycle. Charging transfers energy into stored fields, some of which can return to the generator; net cycle work depends on the voltage-current history and dissipative or radiative losses.
review.calculation_check: The multiplication qV = 10⁻⁸ J is correct for moving 1 nC through a fixed opposing 10 V potential difference. It does not determine cycle energy. For comparison, charging an ideal capacitor from zero to Q = 1 nC at final voltage 10 V stores QV/2 = 5 × 10⁻⁹ J, and its reversible net cycle work is zero. Generally, cycle work is ∮V dq.
review.assumptions: Conventional current and the charge-building instant depicted. No waveform, capacitance, radiation resistance, or charge transferred per complete cycle is supplied.
review.notes: Correct explanation of the pictured directions, but the asserted 10⁻⁸ J of generator work per cycle is unsupported and confuses charge-transfer work with net cycle energy.
review.reviewer: Codex CLI paced physics reasoning review

items.preview: In which situation shown in [[Figure 4]](#Figure4) will the electromagnetic wave be more successful in inducing a current in the wire? Explain. ![Part a of the diagram shows an el…

review.reasoning_check: Figure 4 confirms that the electric field is parallel to the vertical wire in (a) and perpendicular in (b). The longitudinal electric force drives the desired antenna current in (a). In (b), transverse polarization produces little longitudinal response, and a magnetic field parallel to the wire cannot exert a force component along it.
review.calculation_check: The incident longitudinal driving voltage is ∫E·dl ≈ E₀l = (0.100 V/m)(1.00 m) = 0.100 V in (a), versus zero in the ideal orientation of (b).
review.assumptions: A thin straight receiving wire, negligible cross-polarization coupling, and a transverse incident wave whose field is approximately uniform along the wire. The actual current also depends on antenna impedance and loading.
review.notes: Correct polarization comparison and illustrative incident driving voltage.
review.reviewer: Codex CLI paced physics reasoning review

items.preview: In which situation shown in [[Figure 5]](#Figure5) will the electromagnetic wave be more successful in inducing a current in the loop? Explain. ![Part a of the diagram shows an el…

review.reasoning_check: Inspection of Figure 5 supports the intended vertical loop plane containing the propagation direction. In (a), the horizontal magnetic field crosses that plane and produces changing flux. In (b), the vertical magnetic field lies in the loop plane, so its flux is zero. Faraday's law therefore selects (a). The solution uses emf magnitudes, so omitting the orientation-dependent minus sign does not affect this comparison.
review.calculation_check: For Φ = B₀A cos(2πft), the peak emf magnitude is 2πfB₀A = 2.0923 × 10⁻⁵ V. The illustrative wavelength is 300 m, much larger than the approximately 0.1 m loop dimension, validating approximately uniform flux.
review.assumptions: A stationary single-turn loop small compared with the wavelength, the depicted alignment, and negligible pickup from leads or unintended electric-dipole coupling.
review.notes: Correct flux geometry, preferred orientation, and peak-emf calculation.
review.reviewer: Codex CLI paced physics reasoning review

items.preview: Should the straight wire antenna of a radio be vertical or horizontal to best receive radio waves broadcast by a vertical transmitter antenna? How should a loop antenna be aligned…

review.reasoning_check: For reception approximately horizontally from a vertical transmitter, E is vertical and B is horizontal and transverse to the source bearing. A vertical straight wire maximizes its electric response. A vertical loop whose plane contains that bearing has its normal parallel to B, maximizing magnetic flux. Rotating the loop until its normal points toward the source gives a null and the stated two-direction ambiguity.
review.calculation_check: For horizontal rotation through angle θ from the maximum-response orientation, the signed flux and emf scale as cos θ. At 60°, the amplitude is 0.500 of maximum; at 90°, it vanishes.
review.assumptions: A small ideal loop, far-field reception approximately at the transmitter's elevation, preserved vertical polarization, and negligible reflections or parasitic electric pickup.
review.notes: Correct straight-wire alignment, loop maximum and null directions, and angular response.
review.reviewer: Codex CLI paced physics reasoning review

items.preview: Under what conditions might wires in a DC circuit emit electromagnetic waves?

review.reasoning_check: Switching, sparking, commutation, and fluctuating loads create time-dependent charge and current distributions that can radiate despite a DC power supply. A settled macroscopic DC distribution instead produces stationary fields. The inverse switching-time example is acceptable as a rough frequency-scale estimate, rather than a determination of a particular spectral peak or radiation strength.
review.calculation_check: For τ = 1.00 μs, 1/τ = 1.00 MHz, and radiation at that frequency has λ = c/f = 300 m. A transient generally has a broad spectrum; its actual spectrum and coupling cannot be calculated from τ alone.
review.assumptions: Ordinary unshielded circuitry without exact cancellation of radiation. The frequency example is an order-of-magnitude bandwidth estimate; waveform, geometry, return paths, and resonances determine the emitted spectrum and power.
review.notes: Correct transient-radiation conditions. The 1 MHz example is useful only as a rough inverse-timescale estimate.
review.reviewer: Codex CLI paced physics reasoning review

items.preview: Give an example of interference of electromagnetic waves.

review.reasoning_check: Microwave cavity patterns, multipath radio fading, and thin-film colors are valid interference examples. However, the solution presents oven hot spots as necessarily spaced λ/2 apart. That spacing follows for a single one-dimensional standing wave formed by counterpropagating waves, whereas a three-dimensional oven cavity can contain several modes with different spatial patterns. Its hot spots need not have the asserted uniform spacing.
review.calculation_check: At 2.45 GHz, λ = 0.122449 m and λ/2 = 6.12245 cm, correctly calculated for the one-dimensional model. As a counterexample, a standing mode with equal orthogonal wave-number components kx = ky = k/√2 has adjacent antinodes along either coordinate separated by π/kx = λ/√2 = 8.66 cm.
review.assumptions: Stable interference requires sufficient coherence and compatible polarization. The λ/2 result assumes a dominant one-dimensional standing wave; no cavity geometry or mode information establishes that assumption for the stated oven.
review.notes: Valid interference examples, but the specific universal oven hot-spot spacing is an unjustified extension of a one-dimensional model.
review.reviewer: Codex CLI paced physics reasoning review

items.preview: [[Figure 6]](#Figure6) shows the interference pattern of two radio antennas broadcasting the same signal. Explain how this is analogous to the interference pattern for sound produ…

review.reasoning_check: Coherent antenna fields superpose with phase differences set by propagation paths and source phases, just as coherent sound pressures do. For the added in-phase half-wavelength-spacing example, broadside paths are equal and endfire paths differ by half a wavelength, producing enhancement and suppression respectively. Adjusting spacing and phase therefore provides directionality. Inspection of the SVG confirms that the supplied figure itself illustrates multiple constructive directions; the added half-wavelength example is a separate configuration.
review.calculation_check: At 1.00 MHz, λ = 300 m and d = 150 m. The far-field relative phase is 2πΔr/λ: broadside gives zero and endfire gives π. The sound comparison gives 343/1000 = 0.343 m. The SVG has spacing/wavelength = 100/60, consistent with additional constructive directions at sin θ = ±0.6 from broadside.
review.assumptions: Coherent sources with matching polarization and, for exact cancellation, equal received amplitudes. The directional example uses the far field; finite-distance amplitude differences prevent exact cancellation in general.
review.notes: Correct sound analogy and directional-array explanation; the numerical example and inspected figure represent different valid spacings.
review.reviewer: Codex CLI paced physics reasoning review
